content.overview: Promissory estoppel prevents a public authority from going back on a clear promise that induced the promisee to act to their detriment. It applies against the Government subject to limits: it cannot compel an unlawful act, override statute, or defeat overriding public interest properly established.
content.glance: Identify the promise; test clarity and detrimental reliance; ask whether enforcement would compel illegality or defeat public interest; state the equity consequence.
content.study: Indian law recognises promissory estoppel against the Government. The classic requirements are a clear and unambiguous promise, intention that it be acted upon, and detrimental reliance by the promisee. The doctrine is equitable; it yields where enforcement would require the authority to act ultra vires or where a bona fide change of policy in the public interest is shown. Current-law framing: ground the analysis in established Supreme Court authority and the specific promise.

sections.heading: Elements
sections.body: Clear promise; intention that it be acted upon; detrimental reliance by the promisee.

sections.heading: Application to Government
sections.body: The doctrine binds the Government subject to constitutional and statutory limits.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.body: Cannot compel an unlawful act; yields to statute; may yield to overriding public interest.

sections.heading: Relationship with Legitimate Expectation
sections.body: Both protect reliance on public authority conduct; estoppel is promise-and-reliance focused; legitimate expectation is fairness-focused.

examples.title: Tax concession promise
examples.body: Government promises a tax concession to induce investment. The investor acts on the promise. Withdrawal without justification may attract promissory estoppel, subject to statutory and public-interest limits.

hypotheticals.question: Can estoppel compel the Government to act ultra vires?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Estoppel cannot force an authority to do what the law forbids.

hypotheticals.question: Is detrimental reliance always required?
hypotheticals.analysis: Yes in the classic formulation; the promisee must have acted on the promise to their detriment.

distinctions.title: Promissory estoppel vs legitimate expectation
distinctions.right: Representation or practice + fairness under Article 14

misconceptions.correction: It cannot compel an unlawful act or override mandatory statutory provisions.
Only a clear promise intended to be acted upon, followed by detrimental reliance, attracts the doctrine.

cases.issue: Whether promissory estoppel applies against the Government.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Promissory estoppel applies against the Government; a clear promise inducing detrimental reliance can bind the authority subject to limits.
cases.relevance: Leading Indian authority on promissory estoppel against the Government.

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should a promissory-estoppel problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify the promise. II. Test clarity and detrimental reliance. III. Check illegality and public-interest limits. IV. Conclude.

questionsAndAnswers.answer: Promise identified; reliance proved; limits addressed; precise equity relief.

examTips: Emphasise that estoppel cannot compel illegality.
